Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Arjun was a 32-year-old South Asian housekeeper who had come to treatment after months of carrying around a frighteningly clear memory of a mugging that still felt, in his body, as if it had just happened. He had been walking home after an evening shift, cutting through a quieter side street because it was faster, when two men stepped out from between parked cars. One grabbed his bag while the other pinned him against a wall and shoved a forearm hard across his chest. Arjun remembered the sharp sting in his ribs, the pressure in his neck, the roughness of the wall at his back, and the flash of one man’s face leaning in too close. Even now, he could describe the scene in unusually exact detail, down to the color of the jacket the second man wore and the sound of his own breathing turning thin and shallow, yet when he tried to tell it to his wife or to the clinician, he would stall and say that he knew what happened but could not find the words to say it cleanly. The memory seemed to come back all at once, vivid and complete, and with it came a familiar tightening in his chest and a painful ache through the same parts of his body that had been struck during the robbery.

In the weeks afterward, Arjun found that what he believed about other people changed the way the memory lived in him. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that strangers could look ordinary and still be ready to hurt him, and that the world was a dangerous place that could turn on him without warning. Because of that belief, any reminder of being trapped near parked cars, any man stepping too quickly from behind a vehicle, even the sight of a narrow street outside the apartment building where he lived with his wife, could pull the scene back with startling force. At those moments the memory did not feel like a story from the past; it arrived with the same bodily pain and the same helplessness, as if his mind were warning him that danger was still close by. The more clearly the scene returned, the more certain he became that trust itself was foolish. He watched people more closely, read their faces for signs of threat, and each fresh surge of the memory seemed to confirm that his earlier sense of safety had been naïve.

That sharpened vigilance gradually narrowed Arjun’s life. As a housekeeper, he moved through other people’s homes and apartment corridors, but now he avoided taking late assignments and became uneasy when he had to carry cleaning supplies alone in unfamiliar buildings or walk to his car after dark. He would choose longer routes, keep his keys in his hand before leaving a building, and scan every lobby or doorway before stepping through it. Yet the effort to stay ahead of danger kept feeding back into the same fear. When someone crossed close behind him in a hallway, the old memory rose with its vivid details intact; he could feel the old pain, the same pressure in his chest, and his mind immediately returned to the conviction that no one could be trusted. That belief made the memory harder to put into words, because the moment he tried to explain what happened, the scene came back too fast and too complete, leaving him tense and frustrated, convinced that language itself could not contain how unsafe the world felt. Over time he became more withdrawn with coworkers and less willing to stop and chat with neighbors, not because he wanted to be distant, but because distance seemed like the only reliable protection.

By the time Arjun sought help, the robbery had become more than an event he remembered; it had become the lens through which he organized ordinary life. His wife noticed that he was tense every time they went out after sunset and that he bristled when anyone approached too suddenly. Arjun himself felt exhausted by how often the memory intruded and how quickly it pushed him back into the belief that danger was everywhere and trust was misplaced. What finally brought him to treatment was the fear that he was shrinking his world too far to keep himself safe, while still never feeling safe at all. He hoped for relief from the pain that came with the memory and for some way to believe, even a little, that not every person outside their door was a threat.
